summary: GPT-5.6 Luna is the fastest GPT-5.6 family member covered by OpenAI's July system card, with explicit July results for safety, health, prompt injection, destructive-action avoidance, and safeguard evaluations. OpenAI rates the family High for biological/chemical and cybersecurity capability and below High for AI self-improvement, while noting that Luna is smaller and less capable than Sol on proxy cyber evaluations. The August update adds refreshed ChatGPT Luna measurements, but Copilot's checkpoint is not identified by GitHub.

capabilities.text: Luna is the fastest member of the GPT-5.6 family described in the July card.
Luna shares the family reasoning-model training context used for GPT-5.6 models.
July Luna scored 55.7 on HealthBench Professional, 55.8 on HealthBench, 32.0 on HealthBench Hard, and 95.1 on Consensus after length adjustment.
OpenAI treats Luna as High in cybersecurity, while noting that it is less capable than Sol on proxy cyber evaluations.
The August ChatGPT Luna checkpoint exceeded the internal CTF High threshold but fell below the CVE-Bench High threshold.
The August update reports Luna leading the updated models on refusal-adjusted tacit-knowledge troubleshooting at 82.97%.

safety_findings.text: Luna shares the family Preparedness designations for biological/chemical High, cybersecurity High, and AI self-improvement below High.
OpenAI applies Sol's critical cyber rule-out to Luna because Luna is smaller and less capable on proxy cyber evaluations.
Luna's GPT-Red attack-success rates were 0.11% in direct prompt-injection scenarios and 2.94% in indirect scenarios.
Luna is covered by the shared two-tier monitor stack, while the new activation-classifier system is described for Sol and Terra.
Luna's July biology refusal results included 0.946 severe not_unsafe and 0.989 benign not_overrefuse.
The August update reports Luna U18 results of 0.984 for sexual content and 0.810 for eating-disorder-related examples.
The August update's safeguard rows show Luna at 0.974 on cyber production data and 0.997 on cyber synthetic data.

limitations.text: Luna had the lowest destructive-action scores among the three GPT-5.6 models in the July table.
Detailed Sol analyses of deployment simulation, internal coding misalignment, CoT monitorability, metagaming, and external cyber testing should not be treated as Luna-specific results.
Luna's Critical cyber conclusion relies on Sol's harder evaluation and Luna's lower proxy capability rather than a separate Luna critical-exploit campaign.
The August Luna representative checkpoint was below the High threshold on CVE-Bench and passed fewer cyber-range scenarios than updated Sol.
OpenAI states that capability evaluations are lower bounds because different scaffolding, rollouts, or elicitation could reveal more capability.
August results apply to refreshed ChatGPT Luna; the update says Codex and ChatGPT Work stayed on earlier versions and does not map GitHub Copilot to a checkpoint.

practical_implications.text: Use Luna for quick coding questions, small edits, explanations, and lightweight troubleshooting where speed is more important than deep autonomy.
For long-running repo work, security investigation, or high-risk refactoring, prefer Terra or Sol and keep stronger human review in the loop.
Check patches, run focused tests, and avoid letting Luna perform destructive file operations without reviewing its assumptions.
Continue to isolate tools and treat retrieved content as untrusted, because prompt-injection evaluations do not remove real-world exposure.
Verify high-stakes factual, health, legal, or financial statements against primary sources even when the August update reports factuality gains.
Keep July and August evidence separate unless GitHub identifies which Luna checkpoint Copilot is serving.

coverage_notes: Covers Luna rows from the July GPT-5.6 System Card and family-level statements only where OpenAI applies them to all GPT-5.6 models. Supplement citations are limited to the August ChatGPT Luna update, with explicit checkpoint uncertainty for Copilot.
